content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors consider experience replay in continual learning (CL). In their method, each class is represented by a multivariate Gaussian, which is used to sample new "generated" points for subsequent tasks. The method is also combined with two other (known) ideas from the CL literature.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The paper is far below the acceptance threshold for ICML. First, there is an ample literature on "pseudo" replay or "generative" replay where generative models are used in place of a fixed set of samples, starting from (Shin et al., 2017, NeurIPS). The method proposed here is a simplification of these ideas where a GMM is used in place of a "deep" generative model, but this is also common in, e.g., prototype-based CL (https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.09447). Second, the results in Table 1 are very low for almost all methods, pointing to a very poor optimization of the baselines. Third, there is no ablation concerning the different components of the algorithm.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In addition to the points raised above, the paper is basically an unedited draft full of errors and typos, starting from the first sentence: "Continuous learning is a learning scenario that a model that learns data streams without forgetting previously learned knowledge", or later on "(e.g.,due to for privacy issues)". Novelty is almost non-existent (see above), and reproducibility is also lacking because it is unclear how most baselines have been optimized.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is below the acceptance threshold on every count; the novelty is also very limited.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors work on the problem that Continual Learning methods cannot completely replicate the distribution of each task. Concerning this problem, the authors present an approach to represent each class as Multivariate Gaussian Distributions, finding a mean and covariance for each. With these, the authors argue that they can better represent the classes, training only an encoder, the distribution, and the classifier. The encoder is trained on all tasks using an OWM regularization to mitigate forgetting. The authors present positive performance in multiple benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S:
- The idea of using Multivariate Gaussian Distributions is interesting. The motivation of representing the previous tasks in a better way so as not to forget them is a great motivation that has motivated several works in the area.
- The results show that the idea has value.

W:
- Although the authors' motivations are valid, the contributions are not novel. I am not aware of CL works that have specifically used Multivariate Gaussian Distributions. However, some works have used the idea of generating intermediate representations that are not mentioned in the paper. In addition, the idea of making a local adaptation is not novel, as the authors mention, so it is difficult to consider it a contribution.
- Generating input or representations that can fully represent a task is well-motivated. However, it is essential to note that the limitation of the methods that use replay is not in the representativeness of the memory but in the number of elements they save. Sometimes it is helpful only to represent the most representative within each task since, with this, we forget possible outliers.

Q:
- Have you considered applying the idea of ​​distillation to regularize the weights of the model? Instead of using OWM, use similar ideas to Learning without Forgetting to use the vectors generated by Multivariate Gaussian Distributions before and after training.
- Regarding the Local Adaptation. Can you explain in detail how you use it? To adapt the model for sample x_i, first select K nearby classes before generating N samples? Or what do you mean by "test task"?
    - Does Table 3 reflect the accuracy of the selection or training for that number of selected classes? If the latter, it would be helpful to know the accuracy of the selection.
- Why does GAN generate such distant representations concerning the actual distribution? Did you try the proposed method using GANs or VAE?

Recommendations:
- Do not repeat symbols (as in the case of N in Eq4), as it can lead to confusion.
- Placing the names of the methods in Table 1 helps make them more identifiable.
- In Eq 10, if there is an unused term (K_d), it is better to leave it out to avoid adding complexity.
- All abbreviations should be defined. TIL was never defined.
- Table 4 was not explained in the text. However, when mentioning the results, the 500 should be 50.
- The ablation experiments raise more questions than answers. Giving some insights about the results should help explain the results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Motivations and ideas are presented appropriately. However, these are not always accompanied by results that validate them. The ideas presented are also not entirely novel, or the authors weren't able to differentiate themselves from related work.

Some experiments, particularly those of local adaptation, are not entirely clear. With this it becomes difficult the reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Despite the clear motivations, there were no novel ideas or precise results to go along with them.

As a result of reading the document, I leave a few questions for the authors to alleviate any doubts that I had.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is concerned with continual learning. In the past, for sequential learning tasks, prior methods store some samples from past tasks in the memory, and retrieve them for re-training during future tasks. This paper proposes to store the past data in the form of multivariate Gaussian distributions. On the one hand, the distribution is more general than individual samples. On the other hand, the distributions saves memories. The learning of the latent distribution is through EM iterative algorithm. The resulting method is tested on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, with promising performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The general idea of learning distributions for past tasks is novel. This method can help alleviate the catastrophic forgetting issue.
2. Many existing models and methods are included for comparison. The experimental results are generally convincing.

Cons:
1. You should add brief explanations for Figure 2, to explain the example.
2. Since OWM is an important module in your method, you should elaborate on or describe some details.
3. The writing of the paper is not very clear. I suggest you can write pseudo-code for algorithms (like the one in sec 3.2).
4. "...we add a self-supervised loss to let the network learn generalized features...". Your paper should be self-contained. You shouldn't expect reviewers to read another paper to understand your method. But from Figure 3, I suppose the self-supervised loss would be sth like reconstruction? The the whole process mimics VAE?
5. Even you are using distributions, there is still risk of overfitting. And I think the eigendecomposition of the covariance would be very costly?
6. It seems that most datasets you are testing on are not large-scale. What might be the concern to scale the method up?
7. Though I agree the proposed method can help with CF, it might also cause overfitting or limited capacity, which makes it harder and harder to learn for future tasks (if there are a lot of sequential tasks).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The code is not provided, and many details are not well-explained by the paper. It might not be easy to reproduce. I can see the method utilizes the prior works like OWM. It would make the paper better if the descriptions are more self-contained. I think the paper needs major changes in writing. The current writing is not very clear and sometimes confusing.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a meaningful method for continual learning. The general idea is inspiring, but the writing could be refined. Authors should give a more clear high-level description of the method. I'm also a bit concerned with the computation cost of the method. Time costs could be shown.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on continual learning and approaches to solve the catastrophic learning problem by using a memory rehearsal-based solution which involves a multivariate Gaussian. The proposed model consists of an encoder, a classifier and a memory unit. First, the data representation of an incoming task is obtained by using the encoder. In order not to lose any learned knowledge, orthogonal weight modification is used during this process. Then, using the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, means and covariances are obtained and stored inside the memory unit. By using the stored means and covariances, the data is regenerated and a classifier is trained by using the data from the current task and the regenerated data using the information stored inside the memory unit.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
• Memory unit utilization is developed by using obtained information from the data.
• The paper is clearly written.

Weaknesses:
• There are considerable similarities with another paper [1] (see below references). The work in this paper is not novel and there are no citation given to [1]. EM approach, regeneration approach is mentioned in [1].
• The experimental results are not convincing. The paper provides that joint learning on CIFAR- 100 dataset gives 39.97% accuracy when tested on class incremental learning. However, there seems to be more accurate results obtained with CIFAR-100 dataset on class incremental learning. For example, the paper [2] obtains 58.4% accuracy. In addition, the memory size is 10 times lower than this setup. The experiments do not contain the paper [2]. Other relevant papers [3, 4] whose accuracies are listed higher for this dataset are not compared and referenced either.
• Although it is provided that a 6-fold cross-validation is used for every dataset,  the reason for cross-validation is not understood because other papers that this work compares to did not use the cross- validation in their papers. Therefore, it is not clear why 6-fold cross-validation is required for this problem.
• The notation for results is not clear. The paper claims the improvement for CIFAR-10 is 3%p but it is not clear what %p stands for.
• Although there is a reference to [2] and other types of rehearsal based continual learning methods, the experiments do not contain any of the rehearsal methods.
• The setup for the experiments is missing. The code is not provided.
• The effect of memory size is ambiguous. An ablation study containing the effect of memory size should be added for justifying the memory size selection.
• In Table-1, the experimental results for CelebA dataset are written in caption. However, there are not any experiments with CelebA dataset.
[1] Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting with Gaussian Mixture Replay (Pfülb and Geppert, 2021)
[2] Gdumb: A simple approach that questions our progress in continual learning (Prabhu et al., 2020)
[3] Supervised Contrastive Learning (Khosla et al., 2020)
[4] Split-and-Bridge: Adaptable Class Incremental Learning within a Single Neural Network (Kim and Choi, 2021)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is easy to understand. 

Quality: The paper’s language and its figures are in good quality.

Novelty: The work in the paper seems not to be novel since there are considerable similarities with [1].

Reproducibility: The setup for the experiments is not provided and there is not any code provided. Therefore, the results seem to be not reproducible.

[1] Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting with Gaussian Mixture Replay (Pfülb and Geppert, 2021)
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper focuses on continual learning from memory rehearsal aspect by gathering information from observed samples. It justifies the usage of memory unit and its language is easy to understand. However, the experiments are not convincing and due to the lack of the setup, it does not seem to be reproducible. In addition, there are considerable similarities with an earlier paper [1] and the paper does not compare its results with other papers on same domain [2]. Therefore, the paper cannot be recommended.

[1] Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting with Gaussian Mixture Replay (Pfülb and Geppert, 2021)
[2] Gdumb: A simple approach that questions our progress in continual learning (Prabhu et al., 2020)
